facts.statement: Orientalosuchus was a crocodilian that lived during the Late Eocene in Vietnam.
facts.quote: Orientalosuchus is an extinct genus of crocodilian from the Late Eocene that was found in the Na Duong Formation in Vietnam.

facts.statement: Orientalosuchus was a small crocodilian with a blunt, rounded snout and teeth that were pointed at the front and blunt/conical at the back.
facts.quote: Orientalosuchus was a comparably small crocodilian with a blunt and rounded snout and dentition that featured both pointed teeth towards the front of the jaw and blunt, conical teeth in the back.

facts.statement: Orientalosuchus was adapted to eat hard-shelled prey like the many turtles found in its habitat.
facts.quote: Orientalosuchus would have been better equipped to deal with hard-shelled prey, such as the plethora of turtles found in the region.

facts.statement: The genus Orientalosuchus was described in 2019 based on fossils from at least 29 individuals.
facts.quote: The genus was described in 2019 based on the fossil remains of at least 29 individuals

facts.statement: Fossils of Orientalosuchus were discovered between 2009 and 2012 in the Na Duong Basin in Northeastern Vietnam near the Chinese border.
facts.quote: The fossil remains of Orientalosuchus were discovered between 2009 and 2012 during systematic paleontological surveys of the Na Duong Basin in Northeastern Vietnam, near the Chinese border.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen GPIT/RE/09761 is a partial skeleton containing the skull, lower jaw, vertebrae, ribs, limb bones, and over 50 osteoderms.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, GPIT/RE/09761, consists of a partial skeleton featuring the skull, lower jaw and a plethora of postcranial bones including several vertebrae, ribs, various limb elements and over 50 osteoderms.

facts.statement: Orientalosuchus was key to establishing the clade Orientalosuchina, which was initially thought to be early alligatoroids but is now argued to be crocodyloids.
facts.quote: The genus was described in 2019 based on the fossil remains of at least 29 individuals and was key in establishing the clade Orientalosuchina, initially interpreted as a group of early alligatoroids endemic to Asia, although later studies have argued for them actually being crocodyloids instead.

facts.statement: All Orientalosuchus fossils come from the Na Duong Formation, dating from the late Bartonian to Priabonian stages of the Eocene (39 to 35 Ma).
facts.quote: All fossils come from the Eocene (late Bartonian to Priabonian, 39 to 35 Ma) Na Duong Formation

facts.statement: The name Orientalosuchus combines the Latin word for 'east' and the Greek word for 'crocodile' to reference its geographic range.
facts.quote: The name Orientalosuchus is a combination of the Latin word "oriens" meaning "east" and the Greek "soukhos" meaning "crocodile", referencing the overall geographic range of the animal and other orientalosuchins.

facts.statement: Orientalosuchus inhabited tropical to warm-subtropical freshwater biomes including ponds, anoxic lakes, and swamp forests.
facts.quote: During the Late Eocene it would have inhabited the tropical to warm-subtropical freshwater biomes of the Na Duong Formation, which featured ponds, an anoxic lake and swamp forests as some of the primary habitats.

facts.statement: The nostrils of Orientalosuchus faced upwards and were roughly square-shaped with rounded edges.
facts.quote: The nares face upwards (dorsally) and are roughly square-shaped, though with rounded edges and a small indentation formed by the premaxillae forming a process that extends into the opening from the front.

facts.statement: The upper jaw bones of Orientalosuchus had wavy outer edges known as festooning, featuring alternating flaring and constricting.
facts.quote: The maxillae feature sinuous outer edges, a condition known as festooning, with alternating flaring and constricting of the bone.

facts.statement: The front part of the lower jaw where the two halves meet extended back to the fifth tooth and was made entirely of dentary bone.
facts.quote: The mandibular symphysis, the region of the mandible where the two halves meet in the front, extends as far back as the fifth dentary tooth and is formed entirely by the dentary.

facts.statement: The external opening in the lower jaw of Orientalosuchus was very small, only slightly larger than the inner opening.
facts.quote: The external mandibular fenestra of Orientalosuchus is noted as being very small, only slightly larger than the foramen intermandibularis caudalis that lies on the inner side of the jaw.

facts.statement: The upper jaw of Orientalosuchus has five premaxillary teeth and thirteen maxillary teeth on each side.
facts.quote: The dentition of the upper jaw of Orientalosuchus consists of five premaxillary and 13 maxillary teeth on either side.

facts.statement: In the upper jaw, the fourth premaxillary tooth is the largest, followed by the third, while the others are much smaller.
facts.quote: Among the premaxillary teeth, the fourth is the largest, with the third slightly smaller and the remaining teeth all much smaller.

facts.statement: The maxillary teeth in the upper jaw increase in size until the fifth tooth, which is the largest, before decreasing in size.
facts.quote: The maxillary toothrow shows an increase in size leading up to the fifth, the largest of the maxillary teeth, and then a decrease that matches the festooning of the maxilla.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Orientalosuchus has sixteen teeth, with the fourth dentary tooth being the largest.
facts.quote: The lower jaw contains 16 teeth, beginning with three teeth that are close to equal in size followed by the enlarged fourth dentary tooth, the largest in the lower jaw.

facts.statement: The eleventh tooth in the lower jaw is the second largest.
facts.quote: The 11th is the second largest tooth of the lower jaw and followed by several smaller teeth.

facts.statement: The anterior teeth of the jaw are pointed with convex outer surfaces, concave inner surfaces, and prominent ridges running from the tip.
facts.quote: The teeth in the front of the middle of the jaw are pointed with a slightly convex outer (lateral) and concave inner (lingual) surface and several dominant ridges that run from the tip, which are more prominent laterally.

facts.statement: Starting with the tenth maxillary tooth, the teeth become shorter, blunter, and more conical.
facts.quote: Beginning with the tenth maxillary tooth, the dentition switches from long and pointed to short and blunt, appearing more conical in shape.

facts.statement: A large notch between the upper jaw bones accommodates the enlarged fourth tooth of the lower jaw.
facts.quote: A large notch is situated between the premaxillae and maxillae, serving to receive the enlarged fourth dentary tooth.

facts.statement: A gap between the eighth and ninth lower teeth likely accommodates the enlarged fifth upper tooth.
facts.quote: There is furthermore a diastema present between the eight and ninth dentary teeth where the enlarged fifth maxillary tooth of the upper jaw likely comes to rest.

facts.statement: Fossils of Orientalosuchus include more postcranial material than any other known member of its group.
facts.quote: Orientalosuchus also preserves a significant amount of postcranial material, more than other known orientalosuchins.

facts.statement: The preserved skeleton includes most of the spine, ribs, shoulder and pelvic girdles, limbs, and osteoderms.
facts.quote: This includes a large portion of the spine, from the cervical vertebrae to the dorsal, caudal and a single sacral vertebrae, ribs, the shoulder girdle, pelvic girdle, limbs and osteoderms.

facts.statement: Most osteoderms form square dorsal armor plates that lack keels or have only very shallow ones.
facts.quote: The osteoderms are mostly those of the dorsal armor, square in shape and either lacking keels or possessing only very shallow keels.

facts.statement: A single unkeeled triangular osteoderm may have been located on the front side of the body.
facts.quote: A third type of osteoderm is represented by a single triangular element and unkeeled, might have been located anterolaterally.

facts.statement: Orientalosuchus could have grown up to 2 meters long.
facts.quote: Orientalosuchus may have reached a length of up to 2 m.

facts.statement: Initial phylogenetic analyses placed Orientalosuchus as the closest relative to Krabisuchus.
facts.quote: Initially Orientalosuchus was regarded as the sister taxon to Krabisuchus, with the other three positioned in a polytomy.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Orientalosuchina belongs at the base of Alligatoroidea or closer to crocodyloids.
facts.quote: However, not all studies agree with the placement of Orientalosuchina at the base of Alligatoroidea.

facts.statement: A 2024 study recovered Orientalosuchina in two different positions: at the base of Alligatoroidea or as a basal branch of Longirostres outside the crocodyloid-gavialoid split.
facts.quote: Nils Chabrol et al. 2024 managed to recover both hypothesis, with Orientalosuchina composed of Orientalosuchus, Krabisuchus, Eurycephalosuchus and Dongnanosuchus, but lacking the remaining members included by Massonne and colleagues.

facts.statement: Orientalosuchus lived in Vietnam during the Eocene epoch, specifically from the Bartonian to Priabonian stages.
facts.quote: The Na Duong Formation of Vietnam is generally regarded as Eocene in age, corresponding to the Bartonian to Priabonian

facts.statement: The environment where Orientalosuchus lived was a tropical to warm-subtropical swamp containing brooks, shallow ponds, and anoxic lakes.
facts.quote: The formation preserves a tropical to warm-subtropical swamp biome that across its deposition featured a variety of aquatic biomes ranging from brooks and rivulets to an environment dominated by shallow ponds to even an anoxic lake.

facts.statement: The terrestrial habitat surrounding the aquatic environments was a waterlogged swamp forest.
facts.quote: The terrestrial environment would have been represented by a waterlogged swamp forest.

facts.statement: The canopy of the swamp forest where Orientalosuchus lived was estimated to be 35 meters high.
facts.quote: The height of the forest canopy, estimated at 35 m in height.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Orientalosuchus was likely a generalist feeder due to its broader skull compared to other longirostrine species.
facts.quote: Orientalosuchus with its broader skull may have been much more of a generalist.

facts.statement: Evidence of crocodilian bite marks on turtle shells supports the hypothesis that Orientalosuchus preyed on hard-shelled or armoured animals.
facts.quote: This finds some support in the clear presence of crocodilian bite marks on fossil carapace recovered from Na Duong.

facts.statement: While bite marks exist on mammal and crocodilian bones in the same formation, they were likely caused by a large Crocodylus-like animal rather than Orientalosuchus.
facts.quote: Bite marks are also found on the limb bones of mammals and even some crocodilian skulls, though those were more likely created by the large Crocodylus-like taxon rather than Orientalosuchus.

facts.statement: Footprints attributed to Orientalosuchus suggest an animal length of approximately 2 meters, though this may not represent an adult.
facts.quote: Comparing print size with total body length in modern crocodilians suggests that the track macker was likely around 2 meters long.

facts.statement: Orientalosuchus belongs to the parent group Orientalosuchina.
facts.quote: Parent group: Orientalosuchina

facts.statement: Orientalosuchus is classified within the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Orientalosuchus is Orientalosuchus naduongensis.
facts.quote: Type species: Orientalosuchus naduongensis

facts.statement: The genus Orientalosuchus was named by Massonne and colleagues in 2019.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Orientalosuchus (genus), Massonne et al. 2019

facts.statement: The time range for Orientalosuchus is estimated to be between 41.03 and 33.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Bartonian to Priabonian (41.03 to 33.9 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The species name O. naduongensis specifically references the Na Duong coal mine where the fossils were found.
rejected.quote: The species name of O. naduongensis meanwhile more specifically references the Na Duong coal mine where the material was found.

rejected.statement: The lacrimal bone was shaped like a slender triangle and the prefrontal bone was wedge-shaped.
rejected.quote: The lacrimal itself has an elevated medial margin and is overall shaped like a slender triangle and the prefrontal is wedge-shaped.

rejected.statement: A 2019 study grouped Orientalosuchus with other Asian extinct alligatoroids into a clade called Orientalosuchina at the base of Alligatoroidea.
rejected.quote: Phylogenetic analysis at the time found that they were all closely related and together formed a monophyletic clade the team dubbed Orientalosuchina, which they recovered at the base of Alligatoroidea.

rejected.statement: A 2023 study by Ristevski and colleagues found Orientalosuchina deeply nested within Mekosuchinae in some analyses, though this result was supported by only two of eight trees.
